=== projectDescription ===
Mass spectrometry is generally overlooked in the veterinary field despite the potential to yield significant and meaningful data with possible clinical implications. In this study, our team used mass spectrometry to investigate differences between the proteomic profile of a group of dogs diagnosed with an anxiety disorder and a group of control/healthy/non-anxious dogs, thus allowing for inferences to be made in the biological pathways that might be involved or affected in such disorders.
=== sampleProcessingProtocol ===
All dogs were evaluated by a board-certified veterinary behaviorist for the official diagnosis of anxiety disorders or lack thereof, in the case of the control dogs. Venous blood plasma was collected in EDTA tubes, centrifuged at 3000 rpm, 4 °C for 10 minutes to generate plasma. Prior to mass spectrometry analysis the plasma samples were reduced/denatured with 9 M urea / 20 mM DTT in 300 mM Tris, pH 8, at 37 °C for 30 minutes, then alkylated for 30 minutes with 100 mM IAA. Finally, 100 mM Tris, pH 8, was used to dilute the urea and trypsin was added at a 1:20 enzyme:protein (w/w) ratio. Digestion was at 37 °C overnight and quenched with 5.5% formic acid the following day. The 20 plasma samples were digested three times, each in a different month and each set analyzed using a different instrument setup.
=== dataProcessingProtocol ===
Proteome Discoverer 2.4 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used with an FDR of 0.01, followed by data assessment and visualization with Perseus. Data were log2-transformed and imputed using MinDet but no further normalization was applied. Only proteins that were identified in ≥60% of all samples were considered for further data processing. Batch effect was removed using LIMMA R to investigate the possibility of two anxious subgroups. PANTHER, Reactome and the GO Phylogenetic Annotation Project were used to classify genes (and their proteins) found significantly different between the two groups of dogs. Cytoscape and ClueGo+CluePedia were used for functional enrichment, STRING was used to visualize protein-protein interactions and KEGG pathways to visualize relevant biological pathways. In all cases a p-value ≤ 0.05 was used.

=== TITLE ===
Plasma Proteomic Profiling of a Group of Anxious Dogs by LC‐MS/MS: A Case–Control Study
=== ABSTRACT ===
ABSTRACT

Purpose

Anxiety is the most common underlying cause of behavioral problems in dogs, which remain a top reason for relinquishment and euthanasia. Despite its high prevalence, anxiety is often underdiagnosed, partly due to a limited understanding of biological processes and absence of diagnostic biomarkers. Our study aims to address this knowledge gap.

Experimental Design

Plasma from 10 anxious and 10 matched control dogs were analyzed following a label‐free quantitation proteomics workflow based on data‐dependent acquisition using a Thermo Q Exactive Plus coupled to an EASY‐nLC 1200, Vanquish UHPLC, or Evosep One. Data were processed with Proteome Discoverer 2.4 (Thermo), Perseus (Max Planck Institute), Cytoscape and other bioinformatic tools.

Results

Between 279 and 350 proteins were identified, and proteins such as fibrinogen, apolipoproteins, and complement system and coagulation cascade proteins were significantly different between groups. Additionally, we identified two putative subgroups of anxious dogs, suggesting potentially different underlying pathophysiological mechanisms for a single anxiety phenotype.

Conclusions and Clinical Relevance

To our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive clinical in‐depth proteomic profiling of plasma from anxious dogs. Our findings lay the foundation for elucidating the pathophysiology of canine anxiety and for the future validation and establishment of novel candidate biomarkers for disease diagnosis. Novel biomarkers would allow for a more effective and objective diagnosis of anxiety, even when not phenotypically apparent.

Summary

Previous mass spectrometry (MS) studies have found proteomic profile differences in other diseases and other animal species. This is to our knowledge, the first unbiased and comprehensive clinical in‐depth proteomic profiling of plasma from dogs suffering from anxiety disorders.

These findings have an impact on animal health as they set the foundation to elucidate the pathophysiology of canine anxiety so that in the future novel candidate biomarkers can be established and validated, furthering the potential development of new drugs and guiding patient‐specific therapeutic interventions based on biomarker profiles.

In the clinic, novel biomarkers could allow for a more effective and objective diagnosis of anxiety disorders, even when not phenotypically apparent.

Detection and measurement of early stages of anxiety disorders as well as treatment monitoring in pet dogs would allow patients to be treated quicker, before the potential onset of aggression, and a faster recovery, thus improving the welfare of companion animals.
=== INTRO ===
Introduction

Fear and anxiety‐related behaviors represent an inherited strategy, conserved throughout evolution for the ability to sense and avoid potential danger that may threaten survival. Fear differs from anxiety in that it is a response to an immediate, real danger, whereas anxiety is a response to an anticipated threat or potential danger. Anxiety can be triggered by any prospective or imagined situation or stimulus that is deemed dangerous or uncertain to the animal and is characterized by symptoms such as increased heart rate and heavy breathing, as part of the elicited fight‐or‐flight response. Such a response is considered pathological when it is continuous or increased without environmental justification and thus significantly impairs normal daily activities. The biochemical responses resulting in hormonal and immune regulation changes associated with fear and anxiety disorders are poorly understood and not fully elucidated, yet it is known they can negatively affect health by increasing disease frequency, decreasing lifespan, and lowering overall quality of life, thus posing a serious threat to welfare.

The most frequent anxiety‐related behavioral problems in dogs are separation anxiety, generalized anxiety, aggression, fears and phobias, and compulsive disorders, all of which remain significant reasons for relinquishment and euthanasia in dogs. Indeed, behavioral problems have been reported to be as prevalent as in 85% of dogs surveyed, out of which the most common are related to underlying anxiety disorders (at least 74%). The most common individual pet‐related reasons (as opposed to family‐related reasons, such as health issues or allergies, or housing‐related reasons like not enough space or landlord restrictions) for rehoming are aggression (35%) and destruction (29%), both of which could be related to an underlying state of fear, stress, and anxiety. Additionally, a pet dog that suffers from an anxiety disorder directly affects the quality of life of its caretakers. Owners of anxious dogs suffer a high monetary burden because of medication, veterinary care for their pets, and sometimes even property damage. They can become isolated and stressed themselves, which could impact their mental and physical health, and decrease their overall quality of life, thus posing a serious threat to their own welfare. All these factors emphasize the importance of understanding and addressing mental health quickly and effectively in dog patients.

The high occurrence and severe impact of anxiety disorders in pet dogs not only highlights the need to gain further insight into the etiology of such diseases, but also to develop novel, more objective early diagnostic tools, and treatment strategies—including treatment‐progress monitoring—based on the measurement of suitable biomarkers. Biomarkers are features that can be objectively measured and used as indicators of normal biologic or pathogenic processes, or pharmacologic effects to therapeutic treatment. A powerful technique to achieve the above‐mentioned analyses is mass spectrometry (MS).

Mass spectrometry has been successfully used for protein biomarker discovery studies in various diseases, including gammopathies and kidney disorders, pulmonary disease, cancer biology experiments, and even anxiety in a mouse model. A recent study showed plasma protein changes resulting from chronic stress in fish, and human plasma proteomic profiling led to the identification of potential major depressive disorder (MDD) protein markers, which included macrophage migration inhibitory factor, angiopoietin 2, CD40 antigen, tenascin C, von Willebrand factor (VWF), and vascular endothelial growth factor, among others. Additionally, several studies have shown that plasma proteomics can identify biomarkers of disease‐related changes in the brain, such as those seen in Parkinson's disease and sequelae from SARS‐CoV‐2 infection, and even the neurophysiology of social behavior or changes observed due to aging.

In general, however, MS is overlooked in the veterinary and animal‐related fields, even though it has been shown to be a powerful tool for biomarker discovery, disease and disorder therapeutics, and diagnostics. There are very few studies tailored to anxiety disorders, the long‐term effects on the body's biochemistry resulting from coping with anxiety, and any indicators (biomarkers) of such a condition in canine companions. Moreover, the potential for translating these biochemical discoveries from canines to other species, including humans, is intriguing.

The prevalence of anxiety disorders in dogs, the gap in related research, and the lack of biomarkers or a complete understanding of the underlying pathophysiology, have led us to investigate biochemical pathways affected by anxiety disorders in dogs using MS.

We hypothesized that the plasma proteome of anxious dogs would be significantly different from the plasma proteome of non‐anxious/healthy control dogs. Thus, we set out to perform a set of experiments to profile the dog plasma proteome using a discovery proteomics approach to evaluate differences between non‐anxious and anxious pet dog patients with the ultimate objective of identifying novel potential candidate protein target biomarkers for anxiety.
=== METHODS ===
Materials and Methods

Ethics Statement

Experimental protocols and procedures performed as part of this research, with permit number 220801, were approved by the ethical committee: Comité d'éthique de l'utilisation des animaux (CÉUA) operating under the Canadian Council on Animal Care.

Animal Recruitment: Health and Clinical Behavioral Assessment

A total of 20 pet dogs of different breeds, ranging from 4 months to 13 years old were used for this study (Table 1). All dogs, except for one, had been previously neutered/spayed. Initially, 10 anxious dogs that met the criteria stated in Table 2 were recruited, and then 10 matching control/non‐anxious dogs were enrolled in the study. All dogs were required to meet strict criteria, including the official diagnosis of an anxiety disorder, or confirmed lack thereof, depending on whether they were part of the anxious or control group, respectively. All dogs were evaluated through the behavior medicine service at the Veterinary Teaching Hospital of the Faculté de médecine Vétérinaire (FMV), Université de Montréal (UdeM). The 10 anxious dog patients belonged to clients seeking evaluation from a board‐certified veterinary behaviorist for concerning behaviors such as aggressive barking, lunging, biting, displaying fear of inanimate objects or unfamiliar people, house soiling, and destruction in the absence of the owners. The 10 control/non‐anxious dogs were recruited amongst healthy pet dogs belonging to veterinary students and the university community at the FMV and were matched as much as possible to the anxious dogs, except for the 4‐month‐old anxious Great Dane, for which we were unable to find a control/non‐anxious match of similar age. Matching criteria included age, breed, sex, and weight.

Diagnoses were made according to the standards of the American College of Veterinary Behaviorists (ACVB) and included separation anxiety, inter‐ and intra‐specific aggression secondary to anxiety, and generalized anxiety.

Both groups of dogs underwent a thorough 2‐h behavioral assessment, and the details of each dog's life were evaluated. Specifically, the consultation included comprehensive descriptions of their behavior at home, on walks, in familiar and unfamiliar environments, with familiar and unfamiliar people, and with dogs and other species in the presence and absence of their owners. Additionally, each patient's eating, drinking, grooming, and sleeping patterns, as well as play, elimination, and exploratory behaviors, reactivity to noises, including fireworks and thunderstorms, signs of compulsive disorders, and aggressive behaviors were evaluated. Their behavioral development, reproductive history, house training process, training methods used in general, and physical and social environments throughout the development were assessed. Finally, the presence or absence of separation anxiety was evaluated by means of video analysis at home, in the absence of the owners. Control dogs were considered non‐anxious only if all the criteria described in Table 2 for the non‐anxious dogs were met, no anxiety disorder was diagnosed, and the behavioral evaluation was negative for anxiety.

As a final, yet important criterion, both anxious and non‐anxious dogs needed to be in good overall general health for their age. Hence, a detailed medical history was taken, and their medical records were reviewed. All dogs underwent a physical examination and appropriate diagnostics if required to exclude pain and other medically related causes of anxiety. A complete bloodwork (hematology, biochemistry including T4) within normal ranges was necessary, along with not having received any medication in the month prior to sample collection, or any psychotropic medication 3 months prior. A summary of all inclusion criteria can be found in Table 2.

Sample Collection and Handling

We selected blood plasma due to the significant potential of this biofluid to contain strong disease indicators and its collection being relatively non‐invasive and practical, even in anxious canine patients. Venous blood was collected by jugular draw from the 20 dogs recruited following standard operating procedures. Patients were handled following the highest standards of care, using minimal‐stress handling techniques and positive reinforcement, by an experienced team of veterinarians and veterinary technicians, minimizing stress, and maximizing the efficiency of sample collection. All anxious dogs required blood sampling prior to being prescribed appropriate medication(s) to treat their anxiety disorders, so no additional handling than what would be required for regular medication prescription was needed for this study. Similarly, although non‐anxious/control dogs were not prescribed any psychotropic medications and do not require blood sampling as regularly as anxious dogs, it is still recommended to perform routine checks for health assessment, so no additional sampling than what would be recommended was performed for the study. Blood from anxious and non‐anxious dogs was collected in Ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid (EDTA) tubes and then centrifuged at 3000 rpm, 4°C for 10 min to obtain plasma for downstream MS analysis. Plasma was aliquoted into several cryotubes to avoid freeze/thaw cycles, then stored at −80°C until further analysis. All sample handling was performed using standard good laboratory practice techniques to prevent contamination of tubes and samples.

Plasma Sample Digestion

All plasma samples were thawed on ice and prepared following a systematic and unbiased bottom‐up proteomics workflow for untargeted/discovery experiments, involving in‐solution enzymatic digestion techniques as described previously. Briefly, samples were reduced and denatured by incubating 10 µL of each plasma sample with 9 M urea/20 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) in 300 mM Tris, pH 8, at 37°C for 30 min, then alkylated for 30 min at room temperature with 100 mM iodoacetamide (IAA). Finally, the urea concentration was reduced to < 1 M by the addition of 100 mM Tris, pH 8, and trypsin was added to each sample at a 1:20 enzyme:protein (w/w) ratio. Digestion was allowed to proceed overnight at 37°C and then quenched with 5.5% formic acid (FA). The 20 plasma samples were digested three times, each in a different month and each set analyzed using a different instrument setup. Given potentially varying interference characteristics, sensitivities, and reproducibility between LC‐MS setups, we chose three different instrumental setups covering nano‐, micro‐, and high‐flow LC to maximize the number of potentially identifiable biomarker candidates.

Plasma Sample Clean‐Up and Fractionation for EASY‐nLC 1200 and Vanquish UHPLC

Although multiple techniques can be applied to improve protein detection and quantitation in plasma, such as depletion, immuno‐enrichment‐based techniques, and fractionation, they each have limitations. Since depletion relies on antibodies to remove the most abundant proteins, it can lead to variability due to cross‐reactivity and nonspecific binding. This can affect quantitation unpredictably, as low‐abundance proteins could be bound to high‐abundance proteins and be lost during depletion, especially in the absence of internal standards. Non‐specific binding to the filter itself, as well as indirect binding of low‐abundance proteins through interaction with high‐abundance proteins can further deplete proteins of interest. A more specific method at the peptide level, immuno‐MS, could be used instead. However, this often requires generating custom anti‐peptide antibodies, leading to more complications and high costs and is generally more suitable for targeted approaches. Fractionation, on the other hand, represents a more affordable option to reliably increase analytical sensitivity to detect and quantify lower abundance proteins as we have recently shown, and depending on the level of fraction concatenation can result in medium to long overall instrument run times. For all the above reasons, we avoided depletion on purpose and compromised by carrying out an eight‐fraction fractionation technique, followed by concatenation into a final four fractions per sample.

Thus, samples were desalted and fractionated offline using commercially available Oasis HLB µElution plates (2 mg sorbent/well, 30 µm particle size) by Waters, following the manufacturer's instructions. In brief, wells were conditioned with methanol and equilibrated with aqueous 0.1% FA prior to sample loading. Samples were washed three times with LC‐MS grade water and bound peptides were eluted with varying acetonitrile (ACN) percentages (5%, 15%, 20%, 25%, 30%, 35%, 55%, and 75%) with 0.1% FA to yield eight fractions per sample. Fractions were concatenated as follows: 5% with 30%, 15% with 35%, 20% with 55%, 25% with 75% for a final number of four fractions per sample. The concentrated eluates were then evaporated using a speed vacuum concentrator at 50°C, then stored at −80°C until separation and analysis with an EASY‐nLC 1200 and a Vanquish ultra‐high performance liquid chromatography (UHPLC) both interfaced to a Thermo Fisher Scientific Q Exactive (QE) Plus Orbitrap.

Plasma Sample Loading Into EvoTips

EvoTips were prepared for loading following the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, tips were washed with 20 µL of Solvent B (0.1% FA in ACN) and centrifuged at 800 × g for 1 min. Tips were then soaked in isopropanol for 10 s, then equilibrated with 20 µL of Solvent A (0.1% FA in dH2O) and centrifuged at 800 × g for 1 min. Finally, a total of 1 µg of each digested plasma sample was loaded per tip. Note that for the Evosep approach, plasma digests were not fractionated. Tips were centrifuged at 800 × g for 1 min, washed with 20 µL of Solvent A and centrifuged at 800 × g for 1 min. As a last step, tips were filled with 100 µL of Solvent A and centrifuged at 100 × g for less than 1 s to keep the tip resin wet.

LC‐MS Analysis

Dried‐down fractions were reconstituted with aqueous 0.1% FA to a final estimated concentration of 2 µg/µL. Untargeted discovery proteomic analyses were carried out using an EASY‐nLC 1200, a Vanquish Flex ultra‐high performance liquid chromatography (UHPLC), and an Evosep One system, all interfaced to a Thermo Fisher Scientific QE Plus Orbitrap to obtain label‐free semi‐quantitative MS data.

The EASY‐nLC 1200 System was run using an Acclaim PepMap 100 C18 2 cm trap column and a 25 cm × 50 µm C18 PepMap NanoViper column, with a linear 50‐min gradient starting at 0% B up to 40% B (composed of 0.1% FA in 84% ACN). The %B was increased to 80% at 51 min, maintained for 3 min, then returned to 1% by 55 min. Mobile phase A was 0.1% FA in dH2O.

The Vanquish Flex UHPLC was set to maintain the Agilent ZORBAX Eclipse Plus C18 column at 50°C throughout the run and at a flow rate of 0.4 mL/min. The mobile phases A and B were 0.1% FA in dH2O and 0.1% FA in ACN, respectively. The gradient was set to start at 2% Solvent B, switch to 7% B at 2 min, then 11.4% at 10 min, 23.5% at 35 min, 40% at 65 min, 80% at 75 min, and end with a 5 min post wash from 80 to 85 min at 2% B.

Finally, the Evosep One was run using column EV1109 with the 30 samples per day (SPD) method, i.e., a run time of 44 min, using the same mobile phases as the Vanquish UHPLC.

In all three setups, the QE Plus was run in data dependent acquisition (DDA) mode, with a full‐scan resolution of 70,000 and a scan range of m/z 350–1500. The MS2 resolution was set to 17,500, loop count to 10, isolation window to 1.2 m/z, and normalized collision energy (NCE) 28.

Data Analysis and Processing

Raw data files were analyzed to evaluate proteome‐wide fold changes between the non‐anxious and anxious groups. Thermo Fisher Scientific Proteome Discoverer (PD) 2.4 was used as a first step to facilitate data analysis. Unique and Razor peptides were used for quantification and total peptide amount was used as the normalization method. SequestHT (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used as the search engine, against the UniProt database for Canis lupus familiaris (organism ID: 9615), downloaded on September 21, 2022. A maximum of two missed cleavage sites were allowed for trypsin, precursor, and fragment mass tolerances were set to 10 ppm and 0.02 Da, respectively. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine (CAM; +57.021 Da) was set as a static modification, whereas methionine oxidation (MOx, +15.995 Da) and N‐terminal acetylation (+42.011 Da) were set as dynamic modifications. Percolator (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used as the peptide spectrum match (PSM) validator using a strict target false discovery ratio (FDR) of 0.01 and a relaxed target FDR of 0.05.

Further processing was carried out using Perseus v1.6.15.0 for data visualization and statistical analysis. Data were log2‐transformed, filtered based on 60% valid values across all samples, and imputed using the R package ImputeLCMD with the MinDet algorithm. Batch effects were removed using the LIMMA R package as indicated in Section 3. Protein expression level differences that appeared statistically significant between anxious and control groups were determined using a two‐sample 2‐tailed student's t‐test in Perseus with a p value of ≤ 0.02. One‐way ANOVA and Tukey HSD tests were also performed using Perseus, with the p value set to 0.01.

Microsoft Office Excel was used to further visualize and evaluate proteomic differences between the anxious and control dog groups.

Bioinformatic Analyses

Gene Ontology Analysis was carried out using Protein ANalysis THrough Evolutionary Relationships (PANTHER). Thus, biological processes and pathways were mapped and curated by PANTHER and Reactome and the GO Phylogenetic Annotation Project for the classification of the genes (and their proteins) found significantly different between the group of anxious and control dogs. Cytoscape and ClueGo+CluePedia were used for functional enrichment, STRING was used to visualize protein–protein interactions, and KEGG pathways to visualize relevant biological pathways.
=== RESULTS ===
Results and Discussion

Initial Data Assessment

Here we show the identification and relative LFQ of on average ca. 300 dog plasma proteins using raw, non‐depleted plasma by DDA analysis on three different LC‐MS systems (and a total of 417 proteins across the three systems) at medium‐to‐high confidence as determined by Proteome Discoverer 2.4 (Thermo Fisher Scientific), with a strict FDR of 0.01. A total of 279, 291, and 350 proteins were identified across all samples by EASY‐nLC 1200, Vanquish, and Evosep One, respectively (see Figure S1). Of these, 214 proteins were shared across the three instrument setups. The numbers of proteins identified in this study are in line with recent proteomic studies published where Data‐Independent Acquisition (DIA) was used for the quantitation of 400 proteins in non‐depleted canine plasma and surpasses others using DDA or matrix‐assisted laser/desorption ionization (MALDI).

Initial data assessment and visualization were carried out using Perseus, where a set of histograms was generated using the log2‐transformed and MinDet‐imputed signal intensities. It is important to note that only proteins that were detected in ≥ 60% of all samples were considered for further data processing. The data for both the anxious and control dogs show the approximate normal distribution of values obtained from all the systems used (Figure S2) along with the imputed value distribution toward the left side of the histograms, in red. The imputed value distribution is as expected due to the missing data being left‐censored, i.e., missing not at random (MNAR), rather than missing at random (MAR) or missing certainly at random (MCAR). The MNAR imputation strategy is employed when the reason for missing data is most likely due to differences in instrument sensitivity or analytes being below the limit of detection and/or quantitation, as it is rare that a protein is entirely supressed (not expressed) in a given condition. To further assess data distribution, the imputed data were used to generate the box plots shown in Figure S3. Since all samples from both control and anxious dogs showed comparable data distributions in terms of skewness, spread, medians, and number of outliers, no further normalization was applied.

Sample Clustering and PCA

An initial column (sample) Pearson correlation was performed, followed by unsupervised hierarchical clustering analysis using Euclidean distance for initial cluster formation, then average distance for linkage, to visually assess whether the samples would group into separate clusters. As shown in Figure 1, there appear to be clear similarities within the anxious dogs, particularly between Samples A1 and A5, and within the control dogs, forming what seems to be two distinct clusters. Furthermore, we used a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce the dimensionality of such a large data set and visualize data clustering. As shown in Figure 2, the two groups of dogs clustered separately, with A1–A5 being particularly segregated from all the other samples. Interestingly, anxious Sample A10 appeared to be distinct from all other samples in their proteomic profiles, as displayed in both Figures 1 and 2. This sample was obtained from a young Great Dane dog (4 months old), the only puppy in our study. The difference in developmental stage compared to the other dogs may explain the differences observed. Indeed, a recent study showed changes in the human plasma proteome profiles from young adults to seniors, so it is not unlikely that similar changes occur in other species, including canines, which could explain the clear proteomic difference compared to all other samples.

Significantly Different Proteins Between Anxious and Control Dogs

Next, two‐tailed student's t‐tests were performed to determine statistically significant protein concentration differences between anxious and control plasma samples for the three experimental LC setups. As shown in Table 3 and Figure 3, a total of 49 proteins were significantly different between anxious and control dogs in at least one of the three different system setups, and five were found to be differential across the three systems. The diverse sets of differential proteins found between the three LC setups can be explained by variations in LC column composition, flow rate, potential sensitivity, and interference characteristics of each respective LC system. Importantly, however, the proteins that were found to be differentially expressed between the two groups of dogs by two or more of the LC systems, showed the same trend—either always upregulated, or always downregulated (see Table 3). This strengthened the reproducibility of our findings and suggests that the differences in proteins identified between LC setups were indeed due to the differences in the respective LC systems, rather than non‐reproducibility or a true protein absence/presence.

As determined by Gene Ontology Analysis using PANTHER (default p value of < 0.05), several of the differential proteins found between the two groups of dogs are involved in important biological processes, such as biological regulation, cellular processes, response to stimulus, and immune system processes (Figure 4A). An interesting finding was the enrichment of the vitamin D metabolic pathway (Figure 4B), since a recent study with humans showed that low vitamin D levels were associated with increased depression and anxiety symptoms, and in another study, supplementation with vitamin D improved symptoms of anxiety. Most of the enriched proteins, however, are part of other biological pathways such as blood coagulation, chemokine and cytokine‐mediated inflammation, and cholecystokinin receptor signaling (Figure 4B). Further functional enrichment analysis was carried out using Cytoscape and the ClueGO+CluePedia App to confirm the results obtained with PANTHER and derive additional biological meaning from our list of differential genes between the two groups of dogs studied, as shown in Figure 5. The consensus of key properties and equivalent function‐retention of orthologous genes between organisms makes it possible to rely on information available from one species to make novel inferences for genes from another species. Thus, the Homo sapiens gene database was used to generate the figure, using orthologous genes due to the readily more comprehensive proteomic coverage in humans in the literature, compared to dogs. Three separate enrichment analyses were performed, as shown in Figure S4, one per LC‐MS/MS experimental setup. The three setups had the following three major pathways in common: lipid processing/lipoprotein assembly, complement cascade, and coagulation cascade. Moreover, the results from all three experimental setups were combined to provide a summary visualization encompassing all the proteins detected (Figure 5). Across the three LC‐MS/MS methods, most proteins are observed to form an intertwined network of interactions showing the close connectivity of important biological processes, such as the inflammatory response (complement activation), blood coagulation, and lipid transport and are color‐coded according to the corresponding pathways.

Three of the proteins that were found to be differentially expressed between the two groups of dogs, apolipoproteins A‐II (APOA2), C‐1 (APOC1), and C‐IV (APOC4) are involved in the packaging, transport, and metabolism of lipids, including cholesterol, as well as inhibition of cholesterol production. Apolipoproteins may play an important role in anxiety‐related biological pathways, as cholesterol is the precursor for cortisol, a well‐studied biomarker for stress that leads to a variety of physiological effects including the flight or fight response. When environmental stressors cause a stress response in the body, the hypothalamus releases corticotropin releasing hormone (CRH), which triggers the secretion of the adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). This hormone then travels to the adrenal gland and binds to receptors on adrenal gland cells. Cholesterol normally circulates in the blood packaged in high‐density lipoproteins (HDL) containing APOA2. These HDL vesicles bring cholesterol into the cell, and as a result of ACTH‐surface bound signal transduction, cholesterol is transported into the mitochondria, where it is converted to cortisol, and there is evidence of a link between cortisol, cholesterol, and lipoprotein metabolism. It is important to note, however, that we did not measure cortisol in our dog subjects because, although anxiety and stress are related and can co‐occur, for this study we were not interested in measuring stress directly, and cortisol is a direct biomarker for stress. Our focus for this study was to investigate the underlying pathways and mechanisms involved in anxiety and the interplay of such pathways with one another. For instance, we were interested in evaluating whether we could detect differences between the case and control groups in the proteins involved in the neurotransmitter systems, the hypothalamic‐pituitary‐adrenal (HPA) axis and the stress response (or proteins that influence such a pathway), and/or inflammation, which would yield a more detailed picture of the complexity of the different factors that contribute to anxiety. Although high cholesterol has been found in patients with panic disorder, generalized anxiety, and PTSD, the relationship between cortisol and anxiety is not yet fully understood and is likely complex. It is possible that the transport and clearing of cholesterol could potentially be linked to anxiety, and in turn, elevated glucocorticoid levels can affect the metabolism of plasma lipoproteins leading to higher levels of cholesterol and triglycerides. However, measuring cortisol directly does not allow for the differentiation between chronic stress and acute stress, and anxiety has been associated with not only both low and high levels of cortisol, but some studies have also found no association between cortisol levels and anxiety, making it an overall unreliable biomarker for this disorder. Despite the potential unreliability of cortisol as a direct biomarker for anxiety, the literature shows it can have physiological effects involving the heart and blood vessels, such as augmentation of vascular tone, inhibition of tissue repair and remodeling, and hypertension, which can eventually lead to cardiovascular disease.

In our study, the other important pathways from which proteins were found to be differentially expressed between the two groups of dogs were the blood coagulation cascade and the complement system cascade. The coagulation cascade proteins involved included serine protease inhibitors (SERPIN) A1, A5 and D1, fibrinogen b chain (FGB), fibrinogen g chain (FGG), coagulation factor XII (F12), VWF, and plasma kallikrein (KLKB1). The complement system cascade proteins involved included complement components C5, C6, and C8A; complement component 4 binding protein (C4BP); complement factors I (CFI), D (CFD), C1QA; complement C1r subcomponent (C1R); and clusterin (CLU). Importantly, the coagulation and complement system cascades are closely intertwined with one another, as shown in Figure 6.

Overall, the possible involvement of the blood coagulation pathway on anxiety disorders in dogs agrees with the literature, as there is a known association between anxiety and blood coagulation activation as well as fibrinolysis in humans, potentially leading to hypercoagulability, a risk factor for cardiovascular disease. Interestingly, it has been reported that a deficiency in F12 may predispose affected individuals to developing blood clots (thrombi) at an early age. In fact, there is evidence that psychological stress enhances platelet activity, and anxiety has been linked to blood clots. Proteins such as KLKB1 and F12 are involved both in the coagulation system and the plasma kallikrein‐kinin system (KKS; not shown). Importantly, the KKS, where KLKB1 participates in surface‐dependent activation of blood coagulation, fibrinolysis, and kinin generation, has been implicated in neurological disorders and highlighted as a potentially interesting pathway for the development of clinical biomarkers for neurological disease. Moreover, thrombospondin‐1 (THBS1), pro‐platelet basic protein (PPBP; not shown), and CC motif chemokine ligand 14 (CCL14; not shown) which were differential between the two groups of dogs, are involved in the inflammatory response. Interestingly, changes in the levels of fibrinogen and other inflammation biomarkers have been shown to be associated with burnout, depression, and anxiety, and PPBP, which was found to be downregulated in the anxious group compared to the control, has been shown to be downregulated by glucocorticoids, which are secreted in response to stress.

The complement system cascade is involved in the innate immune response and C4BP, a complement system modulator, was found to be downregulated in the group of anxious dogs compared to the control dogs. C4BP regulates the activation of C3 convertase and C5 convertase, which cleave C3 and C5, respectively, releasing products and byproducts involved in inflammation. Thus, the downregulation of C4BP could result in dysfunctional regulation of such enzymes, leading to increased or continuous inflammation. Moreover, C4BP has many additional binding partners, such as pathogens, B cells, endothelial cells, and other cells that may be affected when C4BP becomes downregulated. Importantly, C4BP was found to be a molecular signature of treatment‐resistant depression in MDD patients. Additionally, other proteins such as complement C1q subcomponent subunit A (C1QA), complement components C5, and C8A that were differential between the two groups of dogs are involved in complement activation. Dysfunction in the complement system cascade has also been reported to be related to anxiety, as shown by rodent studies in which mice lacking complement component C3 displayed increased anxiety‐like behaviors compared to wild‐type mice. In addition, inflammation has received significant attention in the context of neuropsychiatric disorders, including depression and anxiety, and cytokines have been documented to impact neurotransmitter systems and their associated circuits when related to anxiety responses. Studies have shown that anxious human patients have increased levels of pro‐inflammatory cytokines compared to healthy subjects, and the activation of an immune response in both humans and rats was observed to increase anxiety‐related behaviors.

Additionally, the cholecystokinin (CCK) pathway is thought to be related to neurotransmission and has been involved in depression‐like behaviors in rats. Indeed, CCK has been proposed as a potential neuromodulator of anxiety and schizophrenia in humans, as γ‐aminobutyric acid (GABA)‐ergic neurons, rich in CCK receptors, manage nerve impulses from the cerebral cortex to the amygdala to trigger anxiety‐like behaviors. Studies with rats further showed that agonists for Group III mGlu receptors led to anxiolytic‐ and antidepressant‐like effects, potentially via inhibition of glutamate release that leads to a reduction in glutamatergic neurotransmission, suggesting the involvement of such receptors in anxiety disorders.

Despite evidence suggesting a link between anxiety and inflammation, additional research is needed to consolidate a cause–effect relationship.

Split of Anxious Dogs in Two Potential Subgroups

While several proteins were identified with significant protein concentration differences between anxious and control dogs, dogs A6–A10 appeared to be different in correlation (Figure 1) and did not readily cluster with anxious dogs A1–A5 (Figure 2). This could mean that targeting these differential proteins alone would not allow to distinguish this subset of anxious dogs from controls for the given set of samples.

We did not want to treat patients A6–A10 as outliers and therefore exclude them, because we originally hypothesized that perhaps this was an example of a false positive diagnosis. That is, dogs that appear to be suffering from an anxiety disorder when in reality it is their “normal” state. This would further highlight the benefit of having a clinical biomarker for anxiety.

Instead, since all samples for the current study had been collected on different days, and by different technicians, we explored the possibility of our data being affected by batch effects. Batch effects can be introduced by different factors, including different sites/laboratories, with different standard operating procedures, sample preservation protocols, procedures for drawing biological samples, which may vary from center to center and over time within center, and between technicians, as well as ambient conditions. Previous studies have shown the impact of different pre‐analytical factors on the measurement of plasma protein biomarkers, with analytes showing higher or lower levels when centrifuged at cold temperatures or collected in CTAD (citrate, theophylline, adenosine, and dipyridamole) tubes, respectively. Delays in centrifugation were further found to impact the analyte levels, depending on the collection tube type used. Thus, biological and technical variability in the analysis of clinical samples remains a recognized limitation in proteomic biomarker studies, including ours.

Even though raw data had been normalized by PD, normalization focuses on correcting the bias generated in each experiment whereas batch effect removal helps reduce any bias generated across batches, including sampling batch effects. Since our samples clustered similarly in the three separate LC setups (Figures 1 and 2), it is possible that any batch effect observed would most likely be due to pre‐analytical factors, rather than caused by instrumentation bias, which would have been, in any case, addressed by the normalization performed in PD. Thus, we applied the LIMMA batch effect removal R package tool through Perseus and generated another set of PCA plots (Figure 7). Interestingly, the PCA results show that Samples A1–A5 and Samples A6–A10 form two separate subgroups within the anxious dogs, possibly due to differing pathophysiologies.

Although the official diagnosis for all dogs in the anxious group was “generalized anxiety,” there were clinical differences between the dogs, as shown in Table 4. For example, four of the five anxious dogs from Subgroup 2 showed aggression, compared to only two of five for Subgroup 1. Additionally, two of five dogs in Subgroup 1 presented with allergies or a dermatological notation, compared to none in Subgroup 2. Since these observations are intriguing, we carried out chi‐square tests with Prism's GraphPad online QuickCalcs to assess whether they were significant. These tests allow us to determine, for example, if there is an association between the dogs presenting with aggression and being part of Subgroup 2. For aggression, the chi‐square with Yates correction showed no statistically significant association, as the chi‐squared was 0.417 with 1 degree of freedom and the two‐tailed p value was 0.5186. Similarly, no association was detected for the dermatologic notation, as the chi‐squared value was 0.625 with 1 degree of freedom and the two‐tailed p value was 0.4292. This statistical result, however, does not necessarily mean that there is truly no association between these clinical presentations and the observed patient segregation, but rather, the number of patients presented in this study was limited and, therefore, unable to yield statistically meaningful data. A larger cohort should be assessed in the future to further dive into the possible and likely underlying biochemical differences between canine patients suffering from “generalized anxiety” that present with different clinical symptoms.

Significantly Different Proteins Between Anxious Subgroups and Controls

To test for statistically significant protein concentration differences between the potential anxious dog Subgroup 1 (Samples A1–A5) and Subgroup 2 (Samples A6–A10), and the control dogs, we performed a post hoc Tukey HSD test for one‐way ANOVA using Perseus for the batch effect‐corrected data (p value ≤ 0.01). An overview of all proteins with significantly different concentrations between the two anxious subgroups and control dogs is shown in Table 5. In total, across the 3 experimental LC platforms, 60 proteins showed significant differences between groups in at least one LC platform.

Next, we performed a functional enrichment analysis with the batch effect‐removed set of differential genes using Cytoscape with the ClueGO+CluePedia App with the same settings described previously. Once again, the coagulation cascade and fibrinolysis appeared to be key differential functional pathways (Figure 8). After batch effect‐removal, however, a few additional, yet interesting functions were enriched, including behavioral response to pain, synapse pruning and regulation of chloride transport, and ATP‐gated ion channel activity.

The behavioral response to pain is linked to the THBS1 and P2RX4 genes. Interestingly, a recent study revealed that recombinant human TSP1, the protein encoded by the gene THBS1, had an antidepressant effect and shows potential as a target for clinical depression treatment. In addition, P2 × 4 surface receptors appeared to regulate anxiety and memory in mice, with an upregulation of such receptors resulting in increased anxiety. Therefore, it is possible that the genes encoding these proteins are involved in canine anxiety as well. The genes C1QC and C1QA, part of the complement system cascade, were enriched in the context of synaptic pruning. The literature has shown that the complement system is indeed involved in synaptic pruning and neurodegeneration. In fact, C1Q and C3 have been shown to play a key role in synaptic circuit refinement during development and adult plasticity in humans, although excessive pruning has been associated with synaptic loss in certain pathological conditions. Excessive synaptic elimination has also been associated with anxiety‐like behaviors as a consequence of neuroinflammation post‐prolonged anesthesia in rats. Finally, chloride transport, or specifically the modulation of chloride channels, has also been investigated in the context of neurological disorders since chloride homeostasis is key in the physiological functions of the central nervous system.

As a means of weighting genes that were found to be differential in multiple MS systems versus a single gene, we assigned a confidence score to each protein based on whether the same significant difference pattern was observed in one, two, or across all three experimental LC platforms (Table 5). Overall, nine proteins showed the same pattern across all three LC systems, therefore, receiving a confidence score of 3. Interestingly, all nine proteins appear significantly different between anxious Subgroup 1 and anxious Subgroup 2. More importantly, six of these nine proteins also showed significant differences between anxious Subgroup 1 and controls and anxious Subgroup 2 and controls. Box‐and‐Whisker plots generated for these six proteins (Figure 9) show the clear difference between the three groups. Thus, CCL14 appears significantly downregulated in anxious Subgroup 1, and upregulated in anxious Subgroup 2, when compared to controls. All of the other five proteins (FGA, FGB, FGG, SERPINA5, and SERPINC1) follow the same trend, where anxious Subgroup 1 is upregulated and anxious Subgroup 2 is downregulated compared to control. The findings suggest that these proteins might be good candidates to distinguish between the subgroups in a potential biomarker panel, whether the difference between the two groups is due to breed, or due to a pathophysiological difference underlying different subcategories of anxiety in dogs. It is important to note that our study did not reveal any clear breed‐specific differences. However, the sample size for individual breeds was too small to allow statistically meaningful comparisons. Genetic studies have shown, however, that while breed‐related differences in protein expression can exist, and they are generally related to physical traits rather than underlying physiological processes or fundamental biological function.

Moreover, 25 proteins showed the same significance pattern in two of the three LC setups (confidence score of 2). Of these, nine proteins showed significant differences between anxious Subgroups 1 and 2, anxious Subgroup 1 and controls, and anxious Subgroup 2 and controls and could therefore be considered as additional potential biomarker candidates for anxiety in dogs. The proteins with confidence scores of 3 and 2 were mapped on a pathway network shown in Figure S5. Of the remaining 26 proteins with a confidence score of 1, 9 proteins showed significant differences across all 3 sample groups in at least one experimental LC setup.

The 24 proteins with significant differences identified across all three conditions (Anxious 1 vs. Anxious 2, Anxious 1 vs. control, and Anxious 2 vs. control) in at least one analytical setup were marked with an asterisk in Table 5 and represent potential candidates for future targeted assay development to validate the findings in the study presented here.
